slides.title: The problem: direct-to-provider LLM access

bullets.text: Every application holds its own provider key. Once there are three apps, nobody can answer "which key is this, and who used it?"
No per-user control: anyone holding a key can call any model. There is no way to grant gpt-4o access to one team and cheap models to another.
No identity in the request path — logs show an API key hash, not a person, so usage cannot be attributed or audited.
Content risk is unmeasured: prompts can leak PII, credentials or secrets, and nothing inspects the request or the response before it leaves.
Provider lock-in: swapping models means changing application code in every service.
Rotating a compromised key means finding every place it was copied — a manual sweep across repositories, CI and laptops.

slides.notes: Frame the problem in operational terms: sprawl, no attribution, no control, no inspection. This motivates a gateway with an identity layer.

slides.title: What AgentPlane is

bullets.text: A single HTTP entry point in front of LLM providers: applications call AgentPlane; AgentPlane authenticates, authorises, inspects, injects the upstream key, forwards, and returns the response.
Identity & access — API keys resolve to users; a deny-by-default RBAC layer decides whether the principal may perform the action.
Secrets — upstream provider keys load through a pluggable secret store (env, file, Vault, AWS, Azure). No key material in application code.
Guardrails — configurable input/output inspection across 10 providers with 4 enforcement actions (detect, warn, redact, block).
Observability — every request becomes an event on an SSE bus and, when capture is enabled, a trace in ClickHouse for analytics and cost reporting.
Operations console — a web control plane for keys, roles, guardrails, usage and live events.
Scope delivered: V0 gateway + request authentication + PostgreSQL persistence + RBAC authorization + secrets backends + guardrails + observability.

slides.notes: One-slide mental model. Everything after this slide expands one of these six capability groups.

slides.title: Architecture — layered modules

shapes.text: Top row = identity plane (who is calling, are they allowed).
Bottom row = data plane (is the content safe, where does it go).

Shared infrastructure: PostgreSQL (users, api_keys, roles, role_permissions, user_roles) · Secret store (env / file / chain / Vault AppRole / AWS / Azure) · Event bus with SSE · ClickHouse (traces, prompt_events, response_events, tool_call_events)

slides.notes: Walk left-to-right: identity plane first (auth → policy → handler), then the data plane (input guardrails → proxy → output guardrails → provider). Bottom band = shared infrastructure. Every package owns exactly one concern.

slides.title: Request lifecycle — one call through the gateway

bullets.text: 1. Client sends POST /chat with Authorization: Bearer ap_live_…
2. auth.Authenticator hashes the presented secret with the server pepper and resolves a user; failure → 401 Unauthorized
3. policy.EnforcementPoint.Require("chat:invoke") runs BEFORE the body is read — static check, 403 policy_denied on deny
4. If the policy engine cannot be evaluated (database error) → 503 policy_unavailable — it fails closed, never silently allows
5. handlers.Chat validates the JSON body, runs input guardrails, then authorises the dynamic permission model:<name> taken from the body
6. proxy.OpenAIProvider loads the upstream key from the configured secret store, attaches it, and forwards the request
7. Output guardrails inspect the response; findings and metrics are emitted to the event bus
8. Response returned to the client — user, model, tokens and cost are recorded as an event (and a ClickHouse trace when capture is enabled)

slides.notes: Emphasise the ordering decision: the static permission is enforced before the body is read (cheap rejection); the model permission comes after body validation because it is data-dependent. Both use the same EnforcementPoint.

slides.title: RBAC design — concepts and matching

bullets.text: Principal
The authenticated users.User resolved by API-key authentication. Roles attach to users, so every key belonging to a user shares that user's permissions.
Permission
An opaque string of the form <resource>:<action> — chat:invoke, model:gpt-4o, model:*, admin:*, *
Role
A named set of permissions (roles + role_permissions). Users receive one or more roles through user_roles.
Matching algorithm — policy.Match(granted, requested)
"*" matches everything (superuser). An exact string matches only itself. A trailing ":*" is a prefix wildcard: model:* matches model:gpt-4o, model:gpt-4o-mini, …
Deny-by-default: a user with no role assignment is permitted nothing. The migration seeds admin and member but deliberately assigns them to nobody.
Model access is a permission rather than a separate allowlist table — one uniform matcher handles endpoints and resources.

slides.notes: The wildcard rule is the core algorithm: exact match, global wildcard, or trailing prefix wildcard. Explain why deny-by-default is the safe failure mode and makes the effective permission set auditable.

slides.title: RBAC enforcement — static, dynamic, fail-closed

rows: Static — needs no request body, so an unauthorised call is rejected before the body is read
Dynamic — the model name comes from the request body

shapes.text: Failure semantics: no user → 401  ·  explicit deny → 403 policy_denied  ·  policy engine error → 503 policy_unavailable.
Chain on /chat: auth → Require("chat:invoke") → handlers.Chat → input guardrails → proxy → output guardrails. A policy error fails CLOSED, so an outage never reads as a violation.

slides.notes: Panel question to expect: why two checks? Cheapest check first (no body read), data-dependent check second. Both flow through the same generic enforcement point, so rate limits, quotas or ABAC can be added later without changing callers (first-deny-wins).

slides.title: RBAC data model — migration 000003

rows: id UUID PK · name TEXT UNIQUE · description · created_at
role_id FK→roles ON DELETE CASCADE · permission TEXT · PK(role_id, permission)
user_id FK→users CASCADE · role_id FK→roles CASCADE · PK(user_id, role_id)

shapes.text: Seeded roles admin → * and member → chat:invoke, model:* are created by ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING but assigned to NOBODY. Idempotent re-runs are safe; cascading deletes prevent orphan permissions; migrations are embedded and applied at startup.

slides.notes: Highlight the deliberate decision: seeding roles without assigning them. Existing users are denied until granted — the safe direction for an upgrade, and it makes the effective permission set auditable.

slides.title: Admin API — roles and users

rows: Create a role (optionally with initial permissions)
Add a permission to a role
Assign a role to a user
Revoke a role from a user

slides.notes: Every control-plane route is wrapped by auth.AdminMiddleware and rejected without the admin bearer token. Example: POST /admin/roles {"name":"gpt4o-only","permissions":["chat:invoke","model:gpt-4o"]} then POST /admin/users/{id}/roles {"role":"gpt4o-only"} — a role limited to one model. Roadmap: replace the static admin token with enforcement of admin:*.

slides.title: Feature — Access Control UI (commit 0718c93)

bullets.text: New web section: Access Control (sidebar index 08) with two tabs
Roles tab — list every role with its permissions; create a role; add or remove individual permissions inline.
Users tab — list every user with their assigned roles; assign or revoke a role per user.
Provisioning integration

The Keys & Vault provisioning form gained an optional role selector. Because role assignment is a different operation from provisioning, the UI performs two steps: it provisions the user and key, then calls POST /admin/users/{id}/roles with the chosen role.
If the second step fails the user and key still exist, and the UI surfaces the error so the role can be assigned later from Access Control → Users. No silent half-provisioned state.
Size: AccessControlView.tsx (365 lines) + api.ts client additions (+94) + App.tsx wiring and new icons — 523 insertions across 5 files.

slides.notes: This slide is the strongest implementation evidence for the branch: a complete UI over the RBAC API, including two-step provisioning and explicit error surfacing.

slides.title: Feature — secrets and the Vault AppRole fix

bullets.text: One interface, five backends selected by SECRET_STORE: env · file · chain · HashiCorp Vault (AppRole) · AWS Secrets Manager · Azure Key Vault.
Callers never read the environment directly — they call config.OpenAIKey(), config.KeyPepper(), config.AdminToken(). Swapping the backend requires no change outside config/ and secrets/.
Bug fixed in this branch: expired AppRole tokens (commit 434a1b7)
Vault AppRole tokens have a TTL. Once expired, the gateway could no longer read the upstream provider key and every chat request failed — a silent outage that appears hours after a healthy startup.
Fix: the Vault store performs a proper AppRole login, retains the lease, renews or re-authenticates before expiry, and re-reads secrets after renewal.
config/store.go was reworked to share the secret-store selection logic; regression coverage added in tests/vault_test.go (+116 lines).
Commit footprint: 273 insertions / 56 deletions across 3 files.

slides.notes: This is the technical-accuracy story: a real production-class failure (token TTL) with a root-cause fix and a regression test, not a cosmetic change.

slides.title: Feature — API-key lifecycle (hash-only)

bullets.text: Provisioning: POST /provision/user creates the user, mints a key, and returns the full key exactly once. Only key_id and the hash are persisted — plaintext is never stored or logged.
Hashing: SHA-256(secret + API_KEY_PEPPER). The pepper is server-side, so a stolen database dump alone cannot be used to forge keys.
Authentication: the presented bearer secret is hashed and matched to the stored hash; the resolved user is attached to the request context and flows into authorization.
Attribution: chat requests are attributed to the authenticated user — this is what makes per-user usage, cost and audit possible.
Revocation: POST /admin/api-keys/revoke by key_id. Last-used timestamps are tracked per key, so dormant or suspicious keys can be identified.
Design split: internal/api owns key generation and persistence, internal/users owns identities, internal/provisioning orchestrates both — none of them know about HTTP.

slides.notes: Hash-only storage plus a server pepper is the security headline for keys. Provisioning is sequential by design; a transactional variant is on the roadmap.

slides.title: Feature — guardrail pipeline (10 providers)

rows: Inspects the request body before forwarding
PII · secrets · prompt-injection · content moderation · Lakera · Prisma AIRS · NVIDIA · Zscaler · AIM · custom rules
Inspects the model response before returning it
Same provider set, applied in the response direction

shapes.text: Guardrails are a registry of independent providers invoked as a chain producing a Decision — the same structural pattern as the policy layer. Identity policy and content policy stay separate packages.

slides.notes: Key technical point: guardrails inspect content, authorization inspects identity. Both use a chain + Decision + fail-closed pattern, keeping the codebase consistent without merging concerns.

slides.title: Feature — observability and analytics

bullets.text: Event bus + SSE: every stage publishes events; GET /events streams them live to the console (Event Log view).

ClickHouse store: four MergeTree tables — traces, prompt_events, response_events, tool_call_events — ordered by (timestamp, organization_id, user_id) and (created_at, trace_id) for time-series analytics.
Capture decisions: a dedicated capture-decision layer decides what may be recorded, so sensitive payloads are not persisted by default.
Hashing and compression: secrets and identifiers are hashed before storage and payloads compressed, keeping the store small and safe.
Usage and cost: pricing configuration maps models to token prices; the gateway records tokens and computes cost per request, aggregated per user in the Analytics and Usage views.
Endpoints: GET /metrics, GET /analytics/traces_count and GET /admin/analytics — the last two behind the admin token.
Observability work also fixed ClickHouse config loading and SQL splitting, including connecting to the default database before running schema migrations.

slides.notes: This is where interim metrics come from. Mention that capture decisions plus hashing are what make storing traces acceptable at all.

slides.title: Deployment — reproducible stack

bullets.text: docker-compose services: vault (dev-mode HashiCorp Vault) · vault-init (seeds AppRole and secrets) · postgres · clickhouse · mock (mock provider API for offline testing) · agentplane (the gateway).
Named volumes vault-creds and pgdata persist Vault credentials and the database between runs.
The gateway image is a multi-stage Go build; migrations are embedded in the binary and applied automatically at startup — schema drift between environments is not possible.
The web console builds to web/dist and is served by nginx (web/Dockerfile + nginx.conf).
A mock provider (testing/, its own Go module with a faker) lets the entire pipeline — auth, RBAC, guardrails, observability — be exercised without spending provider tokens.
dev.sh wires local development: Postgres, API-key auth environment variables and secret-store selection.
.env.example documents every required variable: DATABASE_URL, API_KEY_PEPPER, AGENTPLANE_ADMIN_TOKEN, SECRET_STORE and the provider key location.

slides.notes: Deployment counts as implementation evidence: a reviewer can reproduce the whole system locally, Vault AppRole and ClickHouse included.

slides.title: Technical accuracy — the practices behind the code

bullets.text: Single responsibility per package
Change the provider → only proxy changes. Change the HTTP framework → only handlers change. Change the config source → only config/secrets change.
Provider abstraction
The proxy package hides provider-specific knowledge behind a Provider interface (Name() + Forward()). Adding Anthropic, Gemini, Groq or Ollama means adding a type, not editing handlers.
Configuration abstraction
Secret access sits behind secrets.SecretStore; callers use config.<X>() and never depend on where the secret lives.
Two policy layers, one structural pattern
guardrail = content policy, policy = identity policy. Both are chains evaluated to a Decision, and both fail closed.
Defensive security defaults
Deny-by-default authorization · fail-closed on policy error · hash-only key storage with a server pepper · secrets never logged · admin surface behind a token.
Go engineering and process

Context propagation of the authenticated user · interface-driven boundaries · integration tests guarded by t.Skip so unit runs stay hermetic · conventional commits per module with docs updated alongside the code.

slides.notes: This slide answers 'are the methods and practices correct'. Every claim is visible in the repository structure and commits.

slides.title: Decisions and trade-offs (why it is built this way)

bullets.text: Separate policy package instead of extending guardrail
They change for different reasons — identity/resources vs request content — so keeping them apart preserves single responsibility and lets each evolve independently.
User-level roles instead of per-key scopes
Authentication already resolves a user, so roles need no change to the API-key schema. Per-key scopes remain an additive extension.
Deny-by-default authorization
Access should require an explicit grant: a missing assignment means no permissions, never an implicit allow — and the effective permission set stays auditable.
Model access as a permission, not a separate allowlist table
model:gpt-4o and model:* go through the same matcher as chat:invoke, so endpoints and resources share one uniform authorization model.
Fail closed, and report it distinctly (503 policy_unavailable)
An authorization outage must never read as a permissive state, and must not look like a policy violation either.
Hash-only key storage with a server pepper
A stolen database dump alone cannot forge keys; the plaintext is shown once at provisioning and never persisted or logged.

slides.notes: This slide exists for the Presentation and Clarity criterion: every architectural choice is stated with its justification. If the panel pushes on one, lead with the reason, then name the trade-off it accepts.

Unit coverage sits on the security-critical paths: authentication, RBAC matching and enforcement, proxy forwarding, configuration, observability.
An end-to-end suite (219 test functions) covers handlers, guardrails, PII/secret detection, streaming and the provision → chat → revoke flow.

Interpretation: the newest and riskiest module — authorization — carries the most direct coverage relative to its size.

slides.title: Results — comparison against the current approach

rows: A bearer key with no identity
Key resolves to a user; roles attach to the user
All-or-nothing — any key can call any model
One secret store: env / file / chain / Vault AppRole / AWS / Azure
No inspection of prompts or responses
Input and output guardrails — 10 providers, 4 actions
A key hash in logs; spend unattributable
Per-user tokens and cost, ClickHouse traces, usage views
Change application code in every service
Grant model:<name> — a permission change, not a deployment

slides.notes: Comparison, as the rubric asks. Same request, three different outcomes after this branch: key with no role → 403 policy_denied; key with member → 200; key with a gpt4o-only role asking for another model → 403. Versus purpose-built gateways (LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong AI Gateway): those also proxy and guardrail, so the differentiators here are deny-by-default identity authorization with per-model permissions, the pluggable secret-store abstraction, and per-user cost attribution. State that as 'comparable, with a different emphasis', not as 'better'.

slides.title: Roadmap — what comes next

bullets.text: Enforce admin:* on the control-plane endpoints, replacing the static admin token and closing the loop on the permission model.
Per-API-key scopes on top of user-level roles: a user baseline with optional per-key restrictions.
Additional Policy implementations behind the existing EnforcementPoint — rate limiting, quotas, attribute-based rules — added without touching callers.
Permission caching to remove one database round-trip per request (the current design loads permissions per evaluation).
Provider expansion: Anthropic, Gemini, Groq and Ollama adapters against the existing Provider interface.
True end-to-end SSE streaming to the client (today the upstream stream is coalesced); the guardrail buffer already models the streaming path.
Transactional user and key provisioning, a key-rotation UI, and configurable provider timeouts.
Sequencing rationale: hardening first (admin:*, per-key scopes), then throughput and reach (caching, providers, streaming).

slides.notes: Show the roadmap is sequenced, not a wish list: hardening → efficiency → reach.

slides.title: Anticipated panel questions

bullets.text: Why two authorization checks?
The static chat:invoke check rejects before the body is read; the model:<name> check must come after validation because the model name is request data. Both use one EnforcementPoint.
What if the policy engine or database is down?
It fails closed — 503 policy_unavailable. An authorization outage never becomes an implicit allow.
Existing users lose access after this upgrade. Is that safe?
Deliberate: the migration seeds admin and member but assigns them to nobody. Granting member restores standard access in one documented call.
Can a key be recovered from the database?
No. Only SHA-256(secret + API_KEY_PEPPER) is stored; the plaintext is returned once at provisioning.
Why no rate limiting yet?
Sequenced after authorization hardening. The EnforcementPoint already accepts additional policies (rate limits, quotas, ABAC) without changing callers.
How is correctness demonstrated?
go test ./... — 10 packages ok, 0 failures, 287 test functions. Integration suites need Postgres/Vault, skip without them, and run in the compose stack.

slides.notes: Rehearse these six answers out loud — the rubric explicitly scores responding accurately to panel questions.

slides.title: Demonstration — what we will show live

bullets.text: 1. docker compose up — gateway, Postgres, ClickHouse, Vault and the mock provider come up; migrations apply automatically.
2. Provision a user and mint a key with the admin token — key returned once, hash-only stored.
3. POST /chat with the fresh key and no role → 403 policy_denied; deny-by-default visible in one call.
4. Assign the member role from the Access Control UI → the same request succeeds; the model permission is then evaluated separately.
5. Create a restricted role gpt4o-only and assign it → a request for another model is denied, proving per-model authorization.
6. Revoke the key → subsequent calls return 401 and the console shows the key as revoked.
7. Trigger a guardrail with PII or a credential in the prompt → observe detect → redact → block and the finding in the Event Log.
8. Open Usage/Analytics → tokens, cost and per-user attribution for the calls just made; finish with go test ./... passing.

slides.notes: Keep the demo to these steps; each is a visible pass/fail, which is the most persuasive evidence for implementation and results.

slides.title: Summary

bullets.text: AgentPlane is a working AI gateway: authentication, deny-by-default RBAC authorization, secret-store abstraction, guardrail pipeline, observability and a control-plane console.
The latest branch (feat_rbac) delivered authorization end to end — schema, engine, enforcement middleware, admin API and UI — plus a Vault AppRole token-renewal fix with regression tests.
Correctness is evidenced, not asserted: 10/10 packages passing, 0 failures, 287 test functions and an end-to-end suite; integration tests skip cleanly without external services.
Scale: 8 commits and 89 files on this branch (+10,578 lines); 12,418 lines of Go across 18 packages; 3,893 lines of UI; 17 design documents.
Remaining scope is named honestly — rate limiting, audit logging, multi-provider routing, client-side streaming — and each item has a defined insertion point in the existing architecture.
Thank you — questions welcome.

slides.notes: Close on the three rubric axes: what works, why it is technically right, and what the interim results show.
